Title: It's Time to Pay College Athletes
Subtitle: Text `4`
Author: Zach Dirlam
Content: ...Should college athletes get a piece of the `text($871.6 million)` pie the NCAA brings in
`text(annually)`?
The answer is simple: No, absolutely not.
College athletes are already being paid with an athletic scholarship that is worth
between `text($20-$50,000 per year)`.
Oh, and that does not even begin to factor in the medical and travel expenses, free gear,
top-notch coaching, unlimited use of elite athletic facilities and a national stage to audition
for a job in the professional ranks.
All of those perks are paid for in full by the universities these athletes choose to attend.
Before attempting to discredit some of the cases for compensating players at the college
level, let's take into account all of the things they already receive cost-free.
Athletic scholarships cover just about everything a student-athlete needs to survive for
four years at a major university. Campus housing, daily medical care and free meals via
training table are all included. Tuition and books are covered as well.
None of those things are cheap. It costs `text($57,180)` to attend Duke University. The
University of Texas charges `text($35,776)` for out-of-state enrollees. Even Butler University
charges `text($31,496 per year)`.
This means many college athletes are being reimbursed with nearly as much money as
the average American makes `text(per year)`.
Leaving a text`( college with a degree will help former players earn more money
than those who only have a high school diploma, regardless of whether or not they move on
to a professional sports career.
Students who attain a Bachelor's degree will make text`( more in their lifetimes
than non-graduates.
Traveling around the world is another privilege these student-athletes are afforded. ...
The Fair Market Value Argument
This is `text(one)` of the more common stances pay-for-play supporters take. The idea that
players are not being paid their “fair market value,” however, is a complete myth.
The `text(two)` sports impacted by this argument the most are football and basketball, because
their revenue funds just about every other varsity team at most universities.
These athletes have to be worth `text(millions)`, right? Wrong. College athletes are not worth
a `text(single cent)` on the open market, at least until they are eligible for the NBA or NFL draft.
Changes to the NBA draft eligibility requirements brought an end to high school
athletes heading straight to the professional ranks. Now, NBA hopefuls must be `text(one year)`
removed from high school to enter the draft.
Meanwhile, NFL prospects have to wait `text(three years)` before they can be drafted.
Every student-athlete knows they cannot get paid in college, but if they do not like
it there are other options.
Brandon Jennings was the No. `1`-overall basketball prospect in the country in `2008`.
Instead of attending college, Jennings opted to sign a `text($1.2 million)` deal with Lottomatica
Roma, a professional team in Italy.
The Compton, CA product was drafted `10^text(th)` by the Milwaukee Bucks after playing `text(one)`
season overseas.
Much like the foreign basketball associations, the Canadian Football League does not
have an age requirement. High school graduates wishing to play pro football can head north
and sign a contract right away. ...
Instead of choosing this route, though, NFL and NBA hopefuls take their talents to the
NCAA. The media exposure, coaching and training provided by the universities is far
better than the athletes will receive in foreign markets. Going to classes is simply the
tradeoff for reaping these benefits. ...
Paying College Athletes Will Eliminate Scandals
Contrary to popular belief, the recent scandals involving the Ohio State Buckeyes,
Miami (Fla.) Hurricanes and USC Trojans are not exactly anything new to college athletics.
Paying players will not eliminate any of the greed or determination to win at all costs
that exists in today's society. Cheating will never stop, and it existed at the NCAA level well
before the era of modern technology. ...
The NCAA Has More Than Enough Money to Pay Players
Although the NCAA reels in over `text($800 million per year)`, `text(81 percent)` of which comes
from television and marketing-rights fees, the organization continues to be non-profit.
How is this possible? An astounding `text(96 percent)` of the revenue the NCAA brings in
annually is redistributed to its members' institutions.
This is done through donations to academic enhancement, conference grants, sports
sponsorships, student assistance funds and grants-in-aid. A percentage of revenue is also
added to the basketball fund, which is divided up and distributed to the NCAA tournament
field on a `text(yearly)` basis.
The universities themselves are not exactly rolling in wads of cash, either. `text(Last year)`, only
`22` athletic departments were profitable. Football and basketball bring in the dough, and
every other college sport survives as a result.
Remember this year's Cinderella story in March Madness, the Florida Gulf Coast
Eagles? The university nearly lost money as a result of their run to the Sweet `16`.
`text(Two years)` ago, the Division I Board of Directors approved a `text($2,000)` stipend for college
athletes to cover the “full cost of attendance.” Less than `text(two months)` later, the NCAA's
member institutions repealed the stipend, because they could not afford it.
College athletics may sound like a great business, but in reality only the top-tier
programs are churning out a profit.
I do not agree with everything the NCAA does. However, the evidence shows it is not
the booming business everyone thinks it is. ...
